blocks.markdown: Why the law demands the truth about credit cost

In this lesson you will: **(1)** state the policy behind the Truth in Lending Act; **(2)** define *credit*, *finance charge*, and *creditor* exactly as the statute does; and **(3)** tell which transactions and persons the Act covers. Master the definitions here — every disclosure duty and penalty in the next two lessons hangs on them.

RA 3765 is the **Truth in Lending Act (TILA)**, approved 22 June 1963. Whenever an exam problem mentions TILA, a disclosure statement, or finance charges, this is the governing law. **Remember:** there is no statute-level amendment on record — the implementing detail lives in BSP regulation (notably BSP Circular No. 730).

The State protects borrowers from **not knowing the true cost of credit**. The Supreme Court explains the evil: banks can conceal true cost through hidden charges, uncertain interest rates, and deductions from the loaned amount. Full disclosure lets the debtor **give full consent** and properly evaluate options. **Exam point:** this policy sentence justifies strict construction in favor of disclosure — late or vague disclosure defeats the Act's purpose.

blocks.markdown: 'Board' means the **Monetary Board**. It writes the implementing rules, so always read RA 3765 together with BSP regulation. That is why the disclosure duty in Sec. 4 says 'in accordance with rules and regulations prescribed by the Board.'

**Credit** = any loan, mortgage, advance, discount, conditional sale, installment sale of property or services, rental-purchase, lease/hire/bailment arrangement, lien, pledge, or similar claim — **and any transaction or series of transactions having a similar purpose or effect**.

The definition is deliberately **wide**: anything where payment comes after the transaction counts. A bank loan, a mortgaged loan, a laptop on 12-month installment, a car lease, a pledged advance — all are 'credit.' The catch-all ('similar purpose or effect') stops creditors from relabeling a deal to escape disclosure. **Accounting lens:** if the transaction creates a receivable/payable with a time element and a cost of credit, assume TILA vocabulary applies and test the creditor requisites next.

**Finance charge** *includes* interest, fees, service charges, discounts, and such other charges incident to the extension of credit as the Board may by regulation prescribe. (The statute prints 'may be regulation prescribe' — a [sic] preserved in the provision text.)

The operative word is **'includes'** — the list is open. Interest plus every fee or charge **incident to the extension of credit** that the Board prescribes forms the finance charge. This is the cost population that must be disclosed in pesos and as an annual rate, and that feeds the effective interest rate. A charge with a creative new name is still a finance charge if it is incident to the credit.

**Creditor** = any person **engaged in the business** of extending credit (including one who as a regular business practice lends or sells/rents on time, credit, or installment basis, as principal or agent) **who requires**, as an incident of the credit, **payment of a finance charge**.

Two requisites must **concur**: (1) the **business/regular-practice** element, and (2) a **finance charge** required of the borrower. Banks, financing and lending companies, and stores selling on installment with interest satisfy both. Either element missing means no TILA 'creditor' — and no Sec. 4 duty. Note the definition reaches agents too: one who extends credit for another as a regular practice is covered.

'Person' covers individuals, corporations, partnerships, associations, organized groups, successors and representatives — **including the government and its agencies**. So a state credit program deals with statutory 'persons,' even though Sec. 6(d) later exempts the government itself from the Act's punishments and penalties.

table.caption: Is TILA in play? Test credit first, then creditor
rows: Bank grants a business loan with interest
Covered: loan is credit; bank is in the business and charges a finance charge
Appliance store sells a TV on 12-month installment with service fees
Covered: installment sale of property is credit; store regularly sells on installment and requires charges
Car lease with monthly rentals set by a leasing company
Covered: lease arrangement is credit; lessor in the business, rentals reflect the cost of credit
Neighbor lends P5,000 once, no interest, as a favor
Not covered: isolated act, no business practice, and no finance charge required
Seller gives 30-day trade credit with no interest or fees
Not covered as to that seller: without a required finance charge there is no TILA creditor

blocks.markdown: **Trap:** a problem that screams 'loan' but shows a one-time, interest-free advance is testing the **creditor** definition, not Sec. 4. No finance charge required = no creditor = no disclosure duty. Always check both requisites before enumerating the seven disclosure items.

**Exam:** definition questions reward near-verbatim recall of Sec. 3(2)-(4). Memorize the catch-all ('similar purpose or effect'), the open 'includes,' and the two creditor requisites (business + finance charge). Quote the statute, then apply it to the problem's facts.
